articles.title: ‘Pure arrogance’: anger in Finland as Google illegally fells 250,000 trees for datacentre
articles.summary: Company ordered to stop work at two sites in country, which has found itself at forefront of tech firms’ latest push
articles.body:
Behind a wire fence lies a vast gaping wound of earth. Before Google's arrival a few months ago, an estimated quarter of a million trees occupied the 330 hectares (815 acres) of forest near the town of Muhos in rural northern Finland. Now they are all gone.

After the tech company illegally stripped the entire area to build a datacentre – taking even the top soil with it – all that remains is a vast expanse of mud indented with the trail marks of machinery, puddles and mounds of earth, roots and branches. Residents say that brown water flowing off the site is going into a stream that feeds the Oulujoki River.

"It doesn't end. It goes on and on," says Mari Annala, an ecologist from the Finnish Association for Nature Conservation (SLL), looking at drone footage of the former forest from the perimeter.

With 145 new datacentres at various stages of planning, Finland has found itself at the forefront of the tech companies' latest push. As well as its relative geopolitical and geological stability and abundance of land, the cool climate makes it especially attractive for saving on energy costs.

Earlier this month, Google was ordered by the Finnish Licensing and Supervision Authority (LVV) to temporarily stop work on Muhos and another site about 100km south-east in the village of Otanmäki after it failed to complete the necessary environmental impact assessments before clearcutting the land. The news has prompted widespread outcry and a national reckoning over what role, if any, the country should play in the global rush to build datacentres to keep up with rapid AI development.

Last week, Google's Finland country manager, Antti Järvinen, apologised for the forest clearings but claimed the company had acted "on the best understanding we had of the legislation at the time".

Muhos and Otanmäki are part of a €13bn AI infrastructure project by Google that has attracted criticism from Donald Trump, who would rather the centres were built in the US and has publicly called for the company to reconsider. It is the biggest ever project of its kind in the Nordic country.

The Finnish government, which has presided over deep spending cuts, has encouraged the investment. Last month, when the Google plans were announced, the country's prime minister, Petteri Orpo, said attracting investment was a "top priority" and "the value of the data economy extends far beyond direct investment". He said the Google deal would "deliver lasting benefits for both parties".

But the revelations over Google's misconduct have prompted public concern over what these deals mean for nearby communities, energy prices for Finnish households and Finland's natural environment, a national source of pride. The datacentre push is likely to become a key election issue when Finns go to the polls in April.

In addition to the 250,000 trees felled at Muhos, Annala estimates that an additional 150,000 trees were felled at Otanmäki. Because the trees have been felled illegally, she says wood from the two sites cannot be sold to wood-processing plants.

The move has also prompted questions over why Finland's renewable energy sources are being used to power international corporations.

More than 93,000 people have signed a petition demanding more datacentre regulation and a fee to compensate local communities for environmental damage. Since the scandal broke, Orpo has described what happened in Muhos as a "cold shower".

Hanna Halmeenpää, chair of SLL's board, said she had been incredulous when she discovered Google's law breaking. "At first I couldn't believe it," she said. "I have never heard that any company has done anything like this in Finland." She said the system depended a lot on trust, which she believes Google took advantage of. "They bought the vast land area and they just started to cut it, just like that," she said. "It's pure arrogance and it's amazing."

The speed of developments had shocked the country, she said. "Many people are just watching the news and asking each other: 'What's happening now? What can we do about it? And do we have to take all these datacentre projects in Finland?'"

Jussi Kangasharju, head of computer science at the University of Helsinki, said that while datacentres brought a limited number of jobs, potentially boosting the local economy, the benefits on a national level were minimal. "Really, for Finland, there are no benefits," he said. "They are international companies serving international customers. Very little corporate taxes go to Finland. Datacentres ultimately have very little benefit for others except the datacentre operator."

With legislation still playing catchup, there is a rush to get projects under way as fast as possible.

Some are calling for a centralised body to coordinate datacentre projects, rather than leaving so much of the decision-making down to municipalities that are likely to prioritise the immediate needs of the local area.

In Muhos and Otanmäki, there are people who support the projects, along with the jobs and land taxes they will bring into the local area. But many believe they have been sold short by municipalities.

Antti Jakonen, who lives in Muhos, said that, although the trees felled represented a small fraction of Finland's overall forests, he objected to the manner in which it had been carried out. "It has been done in the wrong way. American style. No sense. No sense at all," he said. The former entrepreneur and fisher wants Google to compensate by helping to restore the local salmon population destroyed decades ago by hydropower.

In Otanmäki, the disruption to nature and to residents' daily lives is being vividly felt. When the trees were felled, the wolves who had lived there came to the village, said Anni Ranta, 53, whose family has lived there for generations.

A former mining village, the area is known for its rare earth elements. Ranta's family live at the centre of the village next to a triangular church spire and a former bar that has been empty for years. The peaceful forest used to extend for miles from the village. Now the sound of building work next to the clearcut Google site reverberates.

"We had wolves coming into the village because all the wild animals moved out of the forest," said Ranta. "They fled. What worries me about the datacentres is also the noise because this is hardrock soil. Even when we are standing here talking," she added, stamping her feet, "it's like a drum."

Such is her strength of feeling against the arrival of Google that she is thinking of moving out. She also fears the datacentre could make the village a target for Russia, with whom Finland shares a long border. "I don't want them here," she said of Google. "I don't want them in Finland at all. I don't like the whole idea of AI and the world changing and the way it's changing. It's going too fast, too soon."

Her father, Pentti Korhonen, a retired wilderness guide, said that since the forest was destroyed, the water in the stream has turned brown. "There is no need at all for datacentres in Finland. No need for datacentres at all," he said.

Vesa Hyyryläinen, chair of the local SLL district, said three-toed woodpeckers nesting in the forest had been pushed out. "All of us nature conservationists are very worried about our Finnish political situation and politics," said the biologist and osprey expert. "I wonder why we have to sacrifice so much of our nature. They give everything away too easily."

He said, however, that he understood why authorities were trying to bring in new sources of investment and jobs, given the region's ageing population. "Young people go to Helsinki and Berlin and Paris," he said. "There are so few people. We have to sacrifice."

Veli-Matti Uski, director general of the ministry of environment, said the government was "monitoring the general development of the [datacentre] sector, [and the] application of its legislation, and is prepared to propose legislative amendments as necessary".

Google said it was working to protect water quality at the Muhos site, and that it planned to plant trees across 130 hectares there. Conservationists say that figure is too low to have any real impact in comparison to the damage done by the tree felling.

A spokesperson said: "We have operated in Finland for 15 years and have always worked to meet or exceed zoning, environmental, health and safety requirements.

"After receiving the LVV letters on 6 October, we stopped preparatory works at Muhos and Kajaani [where the Otanmäki site is located] and have submitted a formal response to LVV confirming this.

"We will fully comply with LVV's requests in this matter. We look forward to maintaining an active, open dialogue with all authorities to strengthen our partnership with Finland and local organisations."
authors: Miranda Bryant in Muhos and Otanmäki

articles.title: London minicabs could be electric by 2030 under new TfL plans
articles.summary: TfL says switching all private-hire vehicles to electric is "vital" in creating a "healthier city".
articles.body:
Transport for London (TfL) has set out new plans which aim to make all minicabs in London fully electric by 2030.

TfL says that currently 70% of all private-hire vehicles (PHVs) in the capital are electric, and says increasing this to 100% is a "vital component" in creating a "healthier city".

The proposals aim for all newly licensed PHVs to be zero-emission from July 2028, with the exception of those that are wheelchair accessible, which would need to be zero-emission from July 2030.

Steve Wright, the chair of the Licensed Private Hire Car Association (LPHCA), said he believed the aspirations were "not achievable", with the cost of charging a vehicle "extremely expensive".

"We have consistently said that most PHV drivers generally don't have the ability to charge vehicles at home," he said.

"The time and cost of charging on-street is extremely expensive, alongside a lack of infrastructure. We will feed back this after speaking to our members via the consultation process."

TfL said the changes were needed as "road transport remains a major contributor to air pollution and carbon emissions in London".

It added that: "Air pollution impacts health in both the short and long term, with Londoners developing life-changing illnesses such as cancer, asthma and lung disease."

As well as minicabs needing to be fully electric, TfL says it will only offer licences to vehicles younger than 10 years old.

TfL forecasts suggest that, within 10 years, the proposed changes could reduce nitrogen oxide (NOx) emissions from minicabs by 9% and carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions by 35%.

Over 18 years, the forecast is these emissions would reduce by 97%.

Reacting to the new plans, Zak Bond, campaign manager at Clean Cities, said: "London has been leading the way in cleaning up its private-hire fleet, but going fully electric has to be the goal.

"It's great to see TfL proposing this crucial next step. These vehicles clock up far more miles than most cars, so switching them to fully electric will make a big difference to the air Londoners breathe.

"A clear deadline gives drivers confidence to plan their next purchase and businesses confidence to invest in charging."

Jemima Hartshorn, founder and director of Mums for Lungs told the BBC it was "a good small step in the right direction," but said more needed to be done, including tackling diesel vans.

"London has still not achieved the air pollution limits it should have achieved in 2010, so any step towards cleaning up our air is welcome," she said.

Christina Calderato, director of strategy at TfL, said: "Private-hire vehicles are a vital component in London's transition to becoming a more sustainable and healthier city with less pollution.

"Building on the progress that has already been made, this consultation sets out our proposals to strengthen those achievements and drive forward the transition towards a zero-emission fleet."

TfL added that although the consultation focused predominately on PHVs, TfL "continues to consider proposals" for a zero-emission requirement for London's black taxis in the future.

The consultation runs until Wednesday 2 December 2026.

articles.title: In 2014, a former banker bought a 475,000-square-foot Connecticut wool mill that had lost 85 jobs; 12 years later, Jacob Long's revived factory employs about 50 people and makes fabric for the US military
articles.summary: A textile factory in Connecticut that shut down in 2013, leaving 85 people without jobs, is now producing fabric for the US military.
articles.body: A textile factory in Connecticut that shut down in 2013, leaving 85 people without jobs, is now producing fabric for the US military. The 475,000-square-foot Warren Mills complex in Stafford Springs was purchased in 2014 by Jacob Harrison Long, a former investment banker who had never run a manufacturing business. Twelve years later, the factory employs about 50 people and supplies material for military uniforms, as Long continues his efforts to rebuild wool manufacturing in the United States.The factory's return to production came at a time when much of America's clothing and textile manufacturing had already moved overseas. Long, however, believed there was still a market for expensive, high-quality fabrics made in the country. Rather than compete with manufacturers producing cheaper textiles in large quantities, he wanted to build a business around specialised woollen and worsted fabrics.His decision has since led to contracts with the US Army, Air Force and Marine Corps. According to CT Insider's report, American Woolen Company began supplying fabric for Army service dress uniforms in 2019. It later expanded its customer base to include other military branches and clothing manufacturers.The business has survived for more than a decade, but Long has a bigger ambition. He wants to see more textile factories operating across Connecticut and New England, a region that once played an important role in American manufacturing. For him, keeping the Stafford Springs mill running is only one part of that effort.What happened to the factory before Long bought it?Warren Mills had been operating for decades before its closure. For approximately 25 years, it had produced fabrics for Italian luxury manufacturer Loro Piana, including woollen and worsted textiles, silk and camel hair.The mill's closure in 2013 came as textile manufacturing continued to decline across the region. According to Connecticut State Historian Andy Horowitz, manufacturers had begun moving operations away from New England as early as the 1920s, partly because labour and other production costs were lower in the southern United States.Long entered the picture after spending around 20 years in Europe, where he had worked in finance. He had noticed that traditional manufacturers in European countries were still producing goods domestically, even as similar businesses struggled in America.He began exploring whether a comparable approach could work in the US textile industry. In early 2013, he acquired the American Woolen Company name, which had once belonged to a prominent American textile business.His original plan did not involve owning a factory. He considered outsourcing production while concentrating on designing and selling fabrics. However, after studying the available manufacturing facilities, he decided that producing the material himself would give the business greater control over quality.That search eventually brought him to Stafford Springs, where the closed Warren Mills complex still had machinery and workers experienced in specialised textile production.How factory returned to productionAfter purchasing its buildings and equipment, Long also needed employees who understood the complicated processes involved in producing and finishing high-quality fabrics. Many of those skills were already available among the people who had worked at Warren Mills before its closure.According to a report by Connecticut Public Radio, the mill's former general manager, Guy Burkhead, said employees had an average length of service of 18 years when the previous business closed. Some had worked there for as long as 40 years.The new company began bringing workers back as production restarted. By September 2014, 21 former employees had been rehired, and additional recruitment was planned.Long also inherited a substantial manufacturing facility, including 40 high-speed spinning looms and other machinery. The factory could produce the specialised fabrics he wanted to market rather than requiring him to build an entirely new operation.Initially, American Woolen concentrated on premium textiles intended to compete with European products. Its business later developed another important source of demand when it secured military contracts in 2019.Rebuilding American textile manufacturing remains difficultAlthough American Woolen has continued operating, the wider industry faces challenges. CT Insider reported that 96.7% of clothing purchased in the United States in 2024 was imported, citing the American Apparel & Footwear Association. Meanwhile, the American Sheep Industry Association estimates that the country exports between 60% and 75% of its wool fibres.Long believes this shows that the United States has both wool supplies and customers, but lacks enough domestic manufacturing facilities to connect the two. "We have sheep and we have consumers. We don't have manufacturing," he told CT Insider.However, expanding production would also require workers with specialised skills and businesses capable of turning fabric into finished clothing.Margaret Bishop, a supply chain expert at Parsons School of Design and the Fashion Institute of Technology, acknowledged Long's achievement in keeping the factory operating for 12 years. She also raised concerns about the limited number of domestic sewing factories and whether younger workers would replace experienced employees approaching retirement.Despite these challenges, Long continues to pursue his plans for New England's textile industry. American Woolen now works with regional manufacturers, including Dow Cover Company in New Haven and New England Shirt Company in Massachusetts.He also sees opportunities among younger consumers interested in durable clothing and second-hand garments. His longer-term aim is to encourage more high-quality textile production in the region.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: At $34 million, a 19,138 sq ft Brookline mansion would beat the $32.5 million sale of Tom Brady and Gisele Bündchen’s former estate, and it comes with 2.06 acres, 16 bathrooms, a pool and a tennis court
articles.summary: In Brookline, where sprawling estates rarely come to market and even fewer command eight-figure prices, one new listing is aiming straight for the top.
articles.body: In Brookline, where sprawling estates rarely come to market and even fewer command eight-figure prices, one new listing is aiming straight for the top. Perched on a hilltop near the Brookline Reservoir, 55 Singletree Road has entered the market at $34 million, setting its sights on a record previously associated with one of New England’s most famous sporting couples.If the seven-bedroom mansion achieves anything close to its asking price, it would eclipse the reported $32.5 million sale of Tom Brady and Gisele Bündchen’s former Brookline estate, making the property one of the most expensive residential sales the town has seen.A mansion built on extraordinary scaleThe numbers alone make 55 Singletree Road a formidable contender. According to the Boston Business Journal, the estate spans 19,138 square feet across 2.06 acres and includes seven bedrooms and 16 bathrooms, comprising 10 full and six partial baths.The property also comes with five fireplaces, a swimming pool, a private tennis court, and a fitness centre. Its elevated position adds another layer to the offering, with listing details cited by Hoodline highlighting a private rooftop terrace with views towards the Boston skyline.Rather than simply being a large suburban residence, the property has been conceived as a private compound with the amenities and proportions associated with a luxury retreat.A carefully engineered custom buildThe mansion dates to 2015, when Acton-based luxury home builder Thoughtforms undertook a substantial two-phase construction project. The company is known for custom residential projects across New England, and the Singletree Road estate reflects that emphasis on scale and bespoke construction.The land has also experienced a dramatic rise in value over the decades. Public records cited by the Boston Business Journal show that the parcel last changed hands in 1993 for slightly more than $1 million. In 2015, the current owner, an LLC linked to a partner at a Manhattan estate-planning firm, took out a $9.1 million mortgage on the property.Tax records cited in the reporting show the home was assessed at approximately $18.96 million in 2025, with an annual property tax bill of $187,133.Taking aim at the Brady-Bündchen recordThe property's ambitious asking price is closely tied to Brookline's luxury real estate history, particularly the former home of Brady and Bündchen.The couple purchased their five-acre Woodland Road property from Pine Manor College for $4.5 million in 2013 before developing a 12,112-square-foot custom residence designed by architect Richard Landry. According to Realtor dot com reporting cited in the Business Journal's coverage, the estate was initially listed for $39.5 million in 2019. After price reductions and a period off the market, it eventually sold for a reported $32.5 million in 2021.At $34 million, the Singletree Road property is therefore positioning itself to become Brookline's new residential benchmark.A luxury listing in a slower marketHoodline's reporting points to signs of cooling in Brookline's wider residential market, with September recording just 25 home sales compared with 45 during the same month a year earlier. Median days on market also rose to 71 days, double the previous year's figure.But trophy homes often operate according to a different set of rules. Their scarcity, scale and highly specific buyer pool can make conventional market indicators less relevant.The listing is being represented by The Sarkis Team at Douglas Elliman Real Estate, whose brokers have experience with Brookline's most expensive properties.Whether 55 Singletree Road achieves its full $34 million asking price remains uncertain. But with its size, amenities and proximity to the town's previous record sale, the estate has already made its ambitions clear: it wants to become Brookline's newest symbol of ultra-luxury living.Images Courtesy: Wikipedia, Instagram, and Town of BrooklineReady to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: Mystery of man found dead in wetsuit deepens as inquest questions ethnicity
articles.summary: An international appeal was launched after the man's body was discovered in a reservoir two years ago.
articles.body:
An unidentified man whose body was discovered in a reservoir in mid Wales two years ago may not have been of white ethnicity as previously thought, an inquest heard.

The body of the man, who was wearing an open water swimming wetsuit, was found by a dogwalker at the Claerwen Reservoir near Rhayader, Powys, in October 2024.

Despite a major international police appeal and the use of ground-breaking facial reimaging techniques, his identity and the cause of his death remain a mystery .

Coroner Patricia Morgan told detectives to analyse a liver sample given to the police two years ago which was never tested, adding she wanted to explore "this further line of inquiry" before reaching a conclusion.

The inquest heard the man's remains could have been in the water for more than three months before they were found.

Tests could determine if he had died before or after he entered the water.

It also emerged that although the force ran the man's DNA through police databases, they did not use commercial DNA sites which are commonly used by people investigating their family history and trying to make connections with long-lost relations.

Det Insp Anthea Ponting told the inquest via videolink that the force considered using such sites at the time but was told it could involve significant resources.

"We were advised we could have results into the thousands. The NCA (National Crime Agency) said they could filter them," she said.

"But it could still lead to a large number of results and a large number of officer hours to work through," Ponting said.

"We wanted to get an ID as soon as possible. We felt that facial recognition might trigger a more far-reaching response."

Initial enquiries gave officers a general idea of the man's age, height and build as between 30 and 60 years old, around 6ft (1.83m), weighing between 202lbs and 220lbs (91.5kg to 99.5kg), and of white European descent.

But in written evidence, forensic orthodontist Dr Sally Andrew said from her examination of his teeth and jaw her finding was that the man "may not have been of white ethnicity".

The hearing was also told an examination of a tag on the wetsuit found marks which could possibly have been a name, but scientific support officers were unable to enhance those marks.

The inquest was adjourned until the test on the liver sample has been carried out.

articles.title: Big Brother fans unhappy as housemate's behaviour called out
articles.summary: Ofcom received thousands of complaints related to Omar El Mayer's behaviour in the Big Brother house.
articles.body:
A Big Brother housemate who prompted more than 7,000 complaints has been spoken to about his on-screen behaviour - but some fans say the show's not doing enough.

Viewers and women's safety charities had been calling on ITV to intervene in Omar El Mayer and Rhianna Collins' relationship after several heated exchanges between the pair.

He was called into Big Brother's Diary Room during Wednesday's episode and told his language and behaviour "could cause offence". He denied dismissing Rhianna's feelings.

ITV has been contacted for comment. The broadcaster previously said "welfare and safeguarding are prioritised throughout the production".

Big Brother contestants live together for 24 hours a day, seven days a week, with almost everything they do captured on camera.

The popular reality show format sees divides form and tensions build as housemates try to avoid being eliminated in weekly votes.

Collins and El Mayer struck up a relationship after entering the Big Brother house but concerns about his alleged "toxic" behaviour had grown among fans.

Monday's episode, which showed a heated exchange between the pair, generated 7,138 complaints, according to broadcast watchdog Ofcom.

Viewers saw Collins break off the relationship before being called to the Diary Room, where she told Big Brother she and El Mayer "have not been good over the last few days".

"Sometimes I don't like the way he speaks to me."

Later, Collins was seen telling El Mayer she didn't want to argue, to which he replied: "Then don't say mad things that you don't mean. It's not fair... sort it out, get it together."

Both Women's Aid and Refuge allege the 21-year-old behaviour towards Collins is concerning and say ITV should do more to protect contestants.

'I've acknowledged my housemate's feelings'

Following the backlash, EL Mayer was called to the Diary Room during Wednesday's episode.

Big Brother told him: "At times it appears that you are dismissing your fellow housemates' feelings and experiences".

"Some of the language used on more than one occasion and the behaviour you have exhibited could cause offence to your housemates or the viewing public."

El Mayer said he "fully understood" the allegations but denied dismissing Collins' feelings.

He said he would challenge people if he disagreed with them, but said he did not believe he had told anyone they weren't entitled to feel however they wanted to.

"Let's be honest here, we're not just talking about housemates, we're talking about my conversations with me and Rhianna," he continued.

He said he'd "done nothing but look out for her" and "didn't walk in with any bad intentions or any malice".

"I've acknowledged my housemate's feelings."

Fans were quick to complain on social media, saying Big Brother should have been firmer and El Mayer should have received a formal warning for his behaviour.

One viewer described it as "a soft talking to" but another said Big Brother made "it clear that his behaviour has not gone unnoticed".

Ofcom said it was assessing the complaints and had not yet decided whether to investigate.

A spokesperson for ITV said earlier this week that housemates receive "respect and inclusion training" and an "extensive briefing" from the show's team on how to prepare for living in the house and to "set out Big Brother's expectations for appropriate behaviour and language".

They said housemates are monitored 24 hours a day and "any instances of inappropriate behaviour are responded to appropriately".

A welfare team is also available to support housemates, the statement added.

articles.title: Sundar the Sailor: Google nixes Trump’s search to name an ocean after himself
articles.summary: TOI correspondent from Washington: The Atlantic Ocean may owe its continued existence, at least under its present name, to Sundar Pichai.
articles.body: TOI correspondent from Washington: The Atlantic Ocean may owe its continued existence, at least under its present name, to Sundar Pichai. By MAGA boss Donald Trump’s own account, the Google CEO rejected his effort to rename the ocean after himself because it touched numerous countries, not just the United States.At a rally in South Carolina on Wednesday, Trump revealed that he had sounded Pichai about his desire to rechristen the Atlantic Ocean and asked him if he can handle it. The Google honcho, according to Trump, told him, “No no no…this time I am not doing it…please don’t ask us to do that” -- because oceans are different from other water bodies in that they skirt many countries.“So I’ll probably pass on that..I think we should keep it as the Atlantic Ocean, right?” Trump said, indicating he had backed off from the idea.Google has not publicly confirmed Trump’s account, which increasingly sound hyperbolic or highly embellished, earning him the sobriquet “Dementia Don" from critics. The episode is the latest installment in the U.S President’s increasingly ambitious campaign to make the world’s geography reflect his understanding of American greatness, which appears to require that the U.S not merely lead the world but also get naming rights over its water bodies.First came the Gulf of Mexico, transformed by executive order into the Gulf of America. Then Mount Denali in Alaska was restored to its former federal name, Mount McKinley. In August, Lake Ontario, shared by the United States and Canada, became Lake America in the federal nomenclature.The U.S President has since mused about renaming the Strait of Hormuz the “Trump Strait” and New Mexico “New America.” A river is apparently also required to complete the collection. The Hudson River has been spared, partly because Trump praised its namesake for his historical exploits, while the Mississippi was left alone because he likes the electoral results in Mississippi.Google Maps has adopted the Gulf of America and Mount McKinley labels for users in the U.S in line with federal naming changes. At a rally in Kentucky last week, Trump boasted that Google had once ignored him but now followed his wishes, declaring that the company was “kissing my ass.” The remark was vintage Trump: crude, triumphant and revealing. The MAGA supremo presented a change in mapping labels as evidence not merely of administrative compliance but of corporate submission, scenes of which he has been rolling out with relish at the White House.In an extraordinary tableau at a White House dinner last month, tech executives whose companies have spent years presenting themselves as independent, disruptive forces in global affairs took turns to pay tribute to the man who controls the regulatory machinery surrounding their businesses. There were obvious reasons for the pilgrimage: Tech companies face antitrust scrutiny, questions about AI regulation, trade and tariff exposure, immigration restrictions affecting their talent pipelines, and enormous infrastructure requirements. A President who can influence the rules of the game is a president no CEO can afford to ignore.Trump’s handling – or taming – of Elon Musk offered another instructive lesson to tech oligarchs. Musk, who boosted and bankrolled Trump to victory in 2024, parted ways with the MAGA boss in 2025 after a public falling-out and briefly challenged him. Trump quickly brought him to heel. For Silicon Valley, the message was hard to miss: cultivate the White House, praise the president’s priorities, announce American investments and avoid becoming the next target of his displeasure.Pichai’s reported refusal to rename the Atlantic may well be a rare instance of a CEO pushing back – politely. It is a small victory for geography and cartography -- and a reminder that even in Washington, where flattery, sycophancy, and adulation is now a flourishing industry, there are limits to what a CEO can put on a map.You use AI every day. articles.title: Newborn twins fight for survival as conflict fuels Yemen's hunger crisis
articles.summary: Raghad and Raad's family had to flee their home on foot because of the fighting between pro-government forces and the Houthis.
articles.body:
From the day they were born, just seven weeks ago, twins Raghad Hassan and her brother Raad have been battling for survival.

They came into the world prematurely, as fighting surged in Yemen's long-running civil war between Houthi rebel fighters and government forces.

When the Houthis reached their village in the Kahboub mountains in south-west Yemen, their family of seven was forced to flee amid bombs, missiles, and drone attacks – the twins protected only by blankets.

What followed was three days on foot heading for the port city of Aden.

"It was very difficult," says their father, Bajash Ali Sagir Hassan, a softly spoken shepherd. "We didn't find cars or transportation. One kind person brought us here [on the fourth day] while others refused."

As the family walked, the twins got weaker, according to their mother Lina. "They were exhausted… there was cold and dust. Their vomiting and diarrhoea got worse."

By the time the newly homeless family arrived at al-Sadaqah hospital in Aden, the twins were barely clinging to life. "Just skin and bone," said a doctor, shaking his head, as he looked at their wasted limbs.

Raad was the sicker of the two - his ribs visible and his chest heaving as he took rapid, shallow breaths. He was barely bigger than the hands of the nurse who carried him gently to be weighed and measured.

Bajash looked on, worry etched on his face. He told us the twins were fed twice a day, but sometimes he could only give them water - after the war drove up the price of baby milk.

The diagnosis came quickly - severe acute malnutrition. That can be as deadly as a bullet.

Malnutrition in Yemen is a crisis within a crisis - another frontline in a devastating civil war. Hunger did not arrive with conflict, but it's spreading with the latest bloodshed.

The United Nations says around 800,000 people can no longer receive lifesaving aid and more than 250,000 have been displaced, after an informal ceasefire collapsed in the summer.

Since then the Houthis have made a lighting advance along the Red Sea coast, and they have now completely cut off Yemen's third largest city, Taiz.

The UN says civilians there are "at grave risk" and lacking food due to soaring prices.

The internationally-recognised government is fighting back against the Houthis - or trying to - with the help of Saudi air strikes.

Caught in the middle of all this are fathers like Bajash, fighting to get help for their children. We saw another mother with a malnourished baby being turned away.

We followed Bajash as he rushed through the corridors, trying to get the all-important admissions slip. He found an ally, a forceful supervising nurse, Aisha Ragab, who had run from the war herself, back in 2018.

"I feel for them," she said, "because I have already lived through the situation myself."

Two beds could not be found, but Aisha was undeterred.

"I will settle this by having the twins share a bed... so that we can save them. By God, I will convince them [the doctors]."

Within an hour the twins were lying on a single bed, their tiny bodies taking up little space.

Lina was feeding them sips of fortified milk from a tiny bottle, but Raad could not keep it down. He was cradled in her arms - his eyes wide and his cheeks sunken. Asked if she thought her twins would recover, Lina replied quietly, "God willing."

As we walked through the unit with its pink walls, some doors were padlocked shut.

There are 22 beds, but staff told us only 13 patients were admitted at a time - the most critical cases - due to the lack of international funding, staff, and equipment.

That's a bitter pill to swallow for Dr Noor Mohammed, a harried young doctor.

"It's sad to say, but we lose patients [because of the conditions]," she says.

"We don't have good equipment like ventilation machines, and oxygen bottles," she adds. "There are no good resources. A lot of laboratory investigations... it's very hard to do them."

A recent flare-up in fighting has left civilians in the firing line.

Even before the latest escalation, the UN calculated that half a million Yemeni children would suffer from severe acute malnutrition this year.

The malnutrition unit in al-Sadaqah hospital is a conveyor belt of suffering. As one severely ill baby leaves, another arrives. And some of those discharged are back all too soon.

"Sometimes a child comes back to us after a week, or two days," says Dr Mohammed. "Sometimes it is the same day. They come back and we admit them and the story begins again."

They return because parents cannot afford proper nutrition or vitamins or antibiotics.

"Every child here, his parents came because they don't have anything," she tells me. "They don't have money or insurance. They are here because they can't afford a private hospital."

She does her best for them, she says, and she cries for them.

Many parents - like Bajash - are trying to outrun both war, and poverty. He is now a shepherd without a flock. When he fled, he had to leave 10 sheep behind. They were his only livelihood.

As doctors monitored his twins, he cared for his three older children - all aged under five. They lingered on a bench in hospital reception without toys, bedding or baggage of any kind. But they could not sleep there.

So, they spent the night outside, on the street - one more family with war wounds that cannot be seen but will disfigure a generation.

articles.title: Websites go dark as AI exposes critical security flaws
articles.summary: Governments and companies around the world shut down websites Thursday as they raced to protect themselves from hacks after artificial intelligence uncovered...
articles.body:
Governments and companies around the world shut down websites Thursday as they raced to protect themselves from hacks after artificial intelligence uncovered critical flaws in a widely used programming language called PHP.

PHP helps run about 70 percent of the world's websites -- from online stores and news outlets to government services -- according to Wiz Research, one of the cybersecurity firms that found the two flaws.

Created in the early 1990s, PHP originally stood for "personal home page" but now means "hypertext preprocessor" and sits underneath popular web design platforms.

"These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history," a Wiz blog post said.

Increasingly powerful AI models can spot weak points in back-end computer code that have gone unnoticed by humans for years.

That has heightened cybersecurity fears, with the number of software vulnerabilities discovered worldwide in 2026 on track to roughly double last year's record total.

PHP programmers released a fix Wednesday, and the US National Security Agency told organizations to patch their sites immediately or pull vulnerable systems offline -- a call echoed by authorities from Japan to the European Union.

A platform affiliated with China's industry and information technology ministry urged the same, warning of "two critical remote code execution vulnerabilities with severe impact" in PHP.

Amazon Threat Intelligence said: "It remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information."

But Ryan Austin, who has worked on PHP issues for cybersecurity firm Calif, told the BBC: "at the moment, it doesn't look like exploitation has taken off or been widespread."

Only sites that run PHP on their own servers are exposed. Many large platforms are built on other programming languages or use operators that could install the fix quickly and were able to stay online.

Rahat Masood, senior lecturer in cybersecurity at the University of New South Wales, Sydney, described the discovery as "quite devastating".

It could allow "attackers to get into your servers without any authorisation, without any username or password", she told AFP.

"Once they are in the servers, they can do anything they want" -- from stealing sensitive information to modifying website content -- she added, urging institutions to "take it seriously."

Government agency sites in countries from Australia to Finland, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom were among those that went dark. Services from insurance firms, transport operators and media outlets were down for emergency maintenance.

Popular apps, including a Pokemon sleep tracker, were also temporarily taken offline while the fix was implemented, while the foundation that runs Wikipedia warned users they could see outages while it addressed the flaws.

"If you run PHP, it is imperative that you update now," the PHP Foundation, which funds developers working on the language, said in a blog post.

Volker Dusch, a security engineer at the foundation, told the Wall Street Journal it was the most serious problem PHP had faced in more than a decade, comparing it to Heartbleed, a 2014 flaw that set off a worldwide rush to patch.

Security firm Calif found the flaws in August using OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol model, as part of an OpenAI-funded audit of PHP's code.

OpenAI said the discovery "marks a new phase, where AI can find security bugs with internet-scale impact."

Wiz, which is owned by Google, said it found them independently weeks later with help from AI models including Google's Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-5.6 Sol.

The flaws had been reported privately to PHP's developers and kept confidential while a fix was prepared.

Details leaked online Tuesday, a day before the planned release of the fix -- prompting the rush to take sites offline before hackers could exploit them.

Steve Kerrison, senior lecturer in cybersecurity at the Singapore campus of James Cook University, told AFP that the fear of hackers using AI to quickly and easily exploit the PHP vulnerabilities had fuelled urgency to react.

So far there has been little evidence of damaging attacks, although data breaches could lead to a wave of so-called "phishing" attacks, where hackers use personal details to steal passwords, down the line.

Larger institutions, from government agencies to news outlets, should be able to fix their websites relatively fast, Kerrison said -- but others may be left vulnerable.

"There are sites, systems and people out there who will have no idea about this and still won't for days, weeks and months," Kerrison warned.

That may include user-run blogs that could be weaponised to spread computer viruses, spam people or distribute malicious content, he said.

articles.body: Bhopal: National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) on Thursday issued notices to the Madhya Pradesh chief secretary and the director general of police (DGP), seeking an action taken report (ATR) within two weeks over allegations that children were involved in Congress leader and former chief minister Digvijaya Singh’s Ujjain-to-Ayodhya yatra and made to raise political slogans.Singh began the yatra from Ujjain on Dussehra.According to a communication issued by NHRC Assistant Registrar Brijvir Singh, the complainant alleged that videos and photographs of the incident were shared on Facebook on Oct 22. The complainant also expressed concern that the children might have been brought to the yatra by offering them money, claiming that their involvement violated child rights and relevant legal provisions.The complaint sought an investigation into the incident and strict legal action against the organisers and others responsible for allegedly involving children in the yatra and making them raise political slogans.The NHRC bench, presided over by its member Priyank Kanoongo, took cognisance of the complaint under Section 12 of the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993.The commission has directed the Madhya Pradesh chief secretary and DGP to inquire into the matter and submit an ATR within two weeks for its consideration, the communication stated.The NHRC has also directed the secretary of Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), Govt of India, to examine the alleged use of photographs and videos of the children and submit an ATR, the communication added.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Bhopal | Silver Rate in Bhopal | Bank Holidays in Bhopal | Public Holidays in Bhopal | Petrol Price in Bhopal | Diesel Price in Bhopal | CNG Price in Bhopal | LPG Price in BhopalStay updated with the latest Bhopal news.
